newsitem.title: USA: More indictments possible in Texaco case.
newsitem.headline: More indictments possible in Texaco case.

text.p: A federal prosecutor said Wednesday there is a "strong possibility" that one or more additional defendants will be charged with planning to destroy evidence in a race discrimination case against Texaco.

So far, only one former Texaco executive, Richard Lundwall, has been indicted in the widely watched case stemming from the defendant's own secret tapes of colleagues discussing the destruction of documents that could have aided the black plaintiffs.

During a scheduling hearing in the Lundwall case, Assistant U.S. Attorney Stanley Okula told the court that there is a "strong possibility" that additional defendants will be named in a new indictment.

He asked for additional time to obtain documents that might be used to bring new charges. Okula said the government is seeking documents that were withheld as part of Lundwall's alleged obstructive behaviour.
U.S. District Judge Barrington Parker set the next hearing for April 30.

Lundwall, 55, the former senior coordinator of personnel services of Texaco's finance department, was indicted March 13 for obstructing justice in the private race discrimination lawsuit filed against Texaco. Lundwall, who has pleaded not guilty to the charge, was indicted after plea negotiations collapsed.
Ironically, the case against Lundwall stems from his own decision to come forward with evidence against himself and others in the discrimination case against Texaco.

In that class action suit, filed in 1994, a group of black employees alleged that Texaco discriminated against them in promotions and pay. Texaco agreed to settle the suit for a record $176.1 million. The accord was approved by a federal judge last month.
When Lundwall was dismissed by Texaco in a downsizing last summer, he gave the tapes to the plaintiffs' lawyers.
Although other executives can be heard on the tapes, Lundwall has been the only one charged. He was the lowest level executive at the meetings that were taped.

A Federal Bureau of Investigation agent's affidavit, which is included in court records, said he had listened to the tapes and heard other Texaco executives, including the company's former treasurer, discussing withholding and destroying documents.
Texaco's treasurer at the time was Robert Ulrich. Ulrich, who has since retired from Texaco, has not been charged by the government.

In January, Texaco permanently suspended all benefits that could legally be cut off to Ulrich and Lundwall and took actions against others heard on the tapes. The company's response occurred after it received a final report from an outside lawyer hired to investigate the matter.
Texaco also gave the report to prosecutors, who have kept it confidential.
